messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Ethnic/Geographic Tension: Arab villages, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Stress: Stress
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mira, a 40-year-old European American woman, had built a steady life with her husband in a suburban home and a demanding career as a data scientist, where long hours at a screen, deadlines, and constant problem-solving were familiar parts of the job. Before the traumatic event, she was used to thinking of herself as composed and competent, someone who could sort through complicated systems and keep herself organized. That sense of herself was shaken during a period of escalating community tension when she witnessed other people caught in a frightening incident near Arab villages, with fire becoming the most unforgettable part of what she saw. She was there in the midst of the chaos, and the sight of flames, along with the charged atmosphere around the villages, left her with a sense of having stumbled into something dangerous and wrong. What stayed with her was not only the scene itself but the feeling that she had failed to protect others when it mattered. In the aftermath, she kept returning to the thought that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, that she should have done more, seen more, or intervened sooner.

In the weeks that followed, Mira found that ordinary stress no longer felt ordinary. When work became busy or a project grew complicated, she experienced a sharp tightening in her body and an urge to throw herself into tasks so she would not be alone with her thoughts. Her days became longer and more crowded with work, not because she felt energized, but because staying occupied gave her a temporary buffer from the memories she did not want to face. Even at home, she would keep busy with chores or another round of email rather than sitting quietly. She described this as working excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, and over time it became one of the main ways she managed to get through the day. Yet the quieter moments still found her. Something in her surroundings could instantly bring back the full memory without warning, and she would be pulled back into the event with little transition, as if the scene had arrived all at once. At times, when she remembered what happened, she also heard things in her head that she had heard during the frightening event, which made the memory feel especially intrusive and difficult to set aside.

The memory itself had a vividness that troubled her. Mira said it felt more real and more alive than memories of ordinary things, as though it had been burned in with a clarity that no daily experience could match. Certain cues carried that quality particularly strongly. Fire or flames were the most obvious trigger, and even a glimpse of a fireplace, a candle, or a flicker of light could make her body react before she had time to think. She also noticed that anything connected to Arab villages or news stories about them could bring the scene back with a force that startled her, because it felt linked to the exact circumstances in which she had first witnessed the event. Stress itself had become a trigger: when work pressure rose, the memory seemed easier to access and harder to contain. In those moments, she would sometimes feel as if the event were happening again, suddenly acting or feeling as if she had been dropped back into it. Strangers approaching her in ordinary situations also made her feel threatened, even when nothing in the present situation was objectively alarming. She became wary in parking lots, on sidewalks, and near the entrance to her building, scanning automatically when someone came toward her.

At home, this wariness showed up in repeated checking. Mira would go back to doors and windows to make sure they were locked, sometimes more than once, unable to trust the first check even though she knew she had done it. The repeated checking was especially noticeable in the evenings, when she and her husband were winding down and she should have been able to relax. Instead, she often moved through the house with a lingering sense that something could still come in or happen if she was not vigilant. Her husband had noticed that she was harder to reach emotionally and that her work took up more and more of her time, though Mira often framed it as needing to stay useful and keep functioning. Privately, she was increasingly troubled by the thought that her life might not be worth living anymore, a thought that frightened her because it felt unfamiliar and heavy, but also difficult to dismiss.

By the time she sought help, Mira was worn down by how much effort it took to get through an ordinary day. She was still working, but the balance of her life had narrowed around productivity, checking, and trying not to be alone with what she remembered. What finally brought her in was the growing concern that she could not keep absorbing these experiences indefinitely, and that the moments when the memory returned so vividly were becoming harder to tolerate. She said she wanted to understand why the event still felt so present and why she could not simply file it away like other hard things in life. More than anything, she hoped to feel safe in her own home and mind again, and she was afraid that if nothing changed, she would remain trapped between the memory that would not fade and the worry that she could no longer trust herself to hold it at a distance.
